prompt.context: Our client, Lizard Insurance, is a US-based auto insurance provider that recently acquired a rival auto insurance company MediumSure. As a part of the acquisition, Lizard Insurance also acquired a subsidiary of MediumSure named TechSize, that provides software for many insurance companies.
prompt.question: Lizard Insurance wants to know what they should do with TechSize, and they've brought us in to help.

clarifying_info.q: Does Lizard Insurance have any experience in the software space?
clarifying_info.a: No – they would need to develop capability.
The TechSize software makes it easier to comply with government regulations when a customer moves from state to state.

clarifying_info.q: Does Lizard Insurance have plans for TechSize?
clarifying_info.a: No – they bought MediumSure for other reasons and don't have plans for TechSize.

clarifying_info.q: How does Lizard Insurance make money?
clarifying_info.a: They sell auto-insurance direct to consumer and collect monthly premiums.
They sell B2B services helping insurance providers comply with government regulations.

exhibits.title: Insurance Software Market Share
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing market share percentages for players in the insurance software market
exhibits.data: Players listed: Software Guru, Insurance App Co, TechSize, Goggle, Next Ten Players. TechSize appears to hold approximately 15% market share. Market shares range from roughly 5% to 30%.

exhibits.title: Insurance Software Market Size
exhibits.shows: Line chart showing total insurance software market size in billions of dollars from 2011 to 2020
exhibits.data: Y-axis from $0B to $6B. The market size appears roughly flat/stagnant, hovering around $5–$5.5B through 2019–2020.

exhibits.title: Information on 2020 Acquisitions
exhibits.shows: Table of three recent acquisitions showing company name, description, 2020 EBITDA, and selling price
exhibits.data: Fill-Your-Forms: EBITDA $25M, Selling Price $125M (5x). Tech Toy Company: EBITDA $1.5B, Selling Price $20B (13x). Insurance App Co.: EBITDA $300M, Selling Price $1.5B (5x).

framework: Binary choice: Keep TechSize or Sell TechSize
Keep options: Do Nothing / Hold; Grow Organically (cross-sell, up-sell); Grow Inorganically (acquire additional players)
Sell options: Partial Sale (license IP, joint venture); Full Sale (spin off into new company, find a buyer)
Evaluate Keep viability: synergies with core business, market attractiveness, investment requirements
Evaluate Sale viability: valuation methods, comparable transactions, market timing

questions.prompt: Analyze the 'Keep' option. What factors should Lizard Insurance consider, and what does the available information tell us?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) Investment requirements – TechSize requires substantial investments and upgrades in the next 2 years to maintain market position. (2) Synergies – No cross-selling/up-selling opportunities because TechSize is B2B and Lizard Insurance is B2C. Switching Lizard's own services to use TechSize would be costly with no meaningful cost reduction. (3) Inorganic growth appetite – Lizard has no appetite for additional acquisitions in TechSize's industry. (4) Market attractiveness (from exhibits) – market is stagnant (flat around $5.5B since ~2015) and fragmented. Conclusion: the Keep option is unattractive; candidate should pivot to analyzing the Sell option.

questions.prompt: If Lizard Insurance decides to sell TechSize, how would you determine its sale value? Walk through your valuation approach.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify multiple valuation methods: DCF (discounted cash flow), Industry Multiples (e.g., EV/EBITDA), and Comparable Transactions. They should ask for comparable transaction data, then be given Exhibit 3.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3 and the market data, calculate an estimated sale value for TechSize.
questions.guidance: Step 1: Identify comparable transactions. A great candidate eliminates Tech Toy Company as non-comparable (children's toys ≠ insurance software). Step 2: Derive EBITDA multiple from remaining comps – Fill-Your-Forms ($125M / $25M = 5x) and Insurance App Co. ($1.5B / $300M = 5x) → implied multiple = 5x EBITDA. Step 3: Estimate TechSize's revenue using Exhibit 1 (15% market share) and Exhibit 2 ($5.5B market size in 2020) → Revenue = 15% × $5.5B = $825M. Step 4: Ask for operating margin – interviewer says 25%. Step 5: EBITDA = $825M × 25% = $206M. Step 6: Sale value = 5 × $206M ≈ $1.03B.

math.setup: TechSize Revenue = Market Share × Total Market Size; EBITDA = Revenue × Operating Margin; Sale Value = EBITDA Multiple × EBITDA
steps: Comparable multiple: Fill-Your-Forms = $125M / $25M = 5x; Insurance App Co. = $1.5B / $300M = 5x → use 5x (exclude Tech Toy Co. as non-comparable)

brainstorming.prompt: What are ways to determine a sale value for TechSize?

categories.name: Intrinsic Valuation
ideas: DCF (Discounted Cash Flow) – project future free cash flows and discount at appropriate WACC

categories.name: Market-Based Valuation
ideas: Industry multiples (EV/EBITDA, EV/Revenue) from publicly traded comparable companies
Comparable transactions – recent M&A deals in similar software/insurtech space

recommendation: Recommend selling TechSize due to limited market potential (stagnant, fragmented market) and lack of strategic synergies with Lizard Insurance's core B2C auto-insurance business
Analysis indicates TechSize could be worth approximately $1 billion based on a 5x EBITDA multiple applied to an estimated $206M EBITDA, consistent with comparable insurance software transactions
risks: Lack of willing buyers at the estimated valuation
Small sample size for the EBITDA multiple (only two truly comparable transactions)
Market conditions may have changed since comparable transactions were completed
next_steps: Conduct due diligence to identify and qualify potential buyers
Engage an investment bank or M&A advisor to run a formal sale process
Validate TechSize's financials and revenue figures ahead of negotiations
